stops.name: Dovia di Predappio, the house by the forge
stops.campa: Benito Amilcare Andrea Mussolini is born in two rented rooms above his father's forge at Dovia, a hamlet of the Romagna. Alessandro, a blacksmith and militant internationalist who reads Bakunin between horseshoes, names his son for the Mexican liberator Benito Juárez and for two Italian revolutionaries, Amilcare Cipriani and Andrea Costa. Rosa Maltoni, the schoolteacher mother, is devout where the father is anticlerical; the household is from its first hour divided between the red flag and the crucifix, a division the son will carry and exploit his whole life.

stops.name: Predappio, the forge and the socialist hall
stops.campa: As a small boy Mussolini sits among the men at his father's forge and at the local socialist circle, listening to Alessandro read aloud from Il Capitale and denounce priests, landlords and the House of Savoy in the same breath. His mother drags him back to catechism and Mass. He is already known in the village for a temper quick to stones and fists with other boys; neighbors mark him early as clever, unruly and incapable of losing an argument gracefully, a boy already rehearsing for larger stages.

stops.name: Faenza, the Collegio Salesiano
stops.campa: Sent to board with the Salesian fathers at Faenza, Mussolini chafes under cassocks, bells and corporal discipline he associates with his father's hated Church. In a dormitory quarrel he draws a penknife and wounds a classmate; the incident, and others like it, follow him through more than one Romagnol school before he is finally steered toward the secular Regia Scuola Normale at Forlimpopoli. The pattern that biographers will trace across his whole career, brilliance yoked to violence at the first provocation, is already visible at ten years old.

stops.name: Forlimpopoli, the Regia Scuola Normale
stops.campa: At the state normal school in Forlimpopoli, boarding on a poor scholarship, Mussolini reads Nietzsche, Sorel, Blanqui and Marx alongside the assigned pedagogy texts, already fluent enough in French to translate. He earns his diploma as a certified elementary schoolmaster at seventeen, the one respectable door open to a clever, penniless Romagnol radical. He takes it, but writes even then to friends that ideas, not a blackboard, are his true instrument, and that a small country schoolroom cannot long hold him.

stops.name: Gualtieri, the first schoolroom
stops.campa: Mussolini takes his first post as elementary schoolmaster at Gualtieri in the Reggio Emilia countryside, lodging in a garret and conducting a public love affair that scandalizes the small town's proprieties. He writes fierce anticlerical, antimilitarist columns for the local socialist press in his off hours, already restless in the classroom. Facing the call-up for compulsory military service he despises, he resigns within months and crosses into Switzerland rather than wear the king's uniform.

stops.name: Lausanne, arrival and arrest
stops.campa: He arrives in Switzerland with almost nothing, sleeping under bridges and, by his own later account, in an empty barrel by the lakeshore before finding casual work as a stonemason's laborer. On 24 July he is arrested in Lausanne for vagrancy and expelled from the canton, the first of several expulsions that will chase him from canton to canton over the following two years as he agitates among Italian emigrant workers and comes to the attention of the Swiss police as a dangerous foreign radical.

stops.name: Lausanne, L'Avvenire del Lavoratore and Pareto's lectures
stops.campa: Settling enough to write, Mussolini joins L'Avvenire del Lavoratore, the emigrant socialist paper edited by Angelica Balabanoff, who tutors him in German and doctrine and finds his oratory already spellbinding and merciless toward rivals. He audits Vilfredo Pareto's economics lectures at the University of Lausanne, reads voraciously, and crosses paths in the exile cafés with the Russian revolutionaries Lenin and Trotsky, who will recall years later, after his desertion to nationalism, the waste of so vehement a talent lost to the cause.

stops.name: Trento, editor for Cesare Battisti
stops.campa: Called into Austrian-ruled Trento by the irredentist socialist Cesare Battisti, Mussolini edits the party's L'Avvenire del Lavoratore and writes for Battisti's own paper Il Popolo, serializing there a lurid anticlerical novel, Claudia Particella, l'amante del cardinale. He agitates openly for Trento's return to Italy, watched now by the Austro-Hungarian police, and finds in Battisti, who will later die on the gallows as a wartime traitor to Austria, a model of conviction backed by the willingness to die for it.

stops.name: Trento, expelled from Austria-Hungary
stops.campa: Convicted under the press laws for inciting irredentism, Mussolini is expelled from Austrian territory and marched to the Italian frontier that autumn. He carries out of Trento a personal grudge against the Habsburg empire that intervention propaganda will later put to use, and a taste for exile worn as proof of conviction rather than shame. He settles in September at Forlì to take up the secretaryship of the local Socialist Party section, his name now known well beyond the Romagna.

stops.name: Forlì, La Lotta di Classe and Rachele Guidi
stops.campa: As secretary of the Forlì socialist section Mussolini edits La Lotta di Classe, denouncing Italy's colonial war in Libya and the reformist compromises of the party's moderate wing. He takes as his companion Rachele Guidi, daughter of his father's own mistress, in a Romagnol union at first without priest or magistrate; a daughter, Edda, is born to them that year. His name is now attached, in Socialist Party circles nationally, to the uncompromising revolutionary line against ministerialism and monarchy alike.

stops.name: Milan, editor of Avanti!
stops.campa: At twenty-nine, on the strength of his intransigence at the stormy Reggio Emilia congress that expelled the party's reformist right, Mussolini is named editor of Avanti!, Italian socialism's national daily, and moves it to Milan. Circulation triples under his hand; his columns against the Libyan war and against compromise with the liberal state make him the idol of the party's revolutionary wing and its single most closely watched figure, socialist and prefect alike wondering how far his appetite for confrontation will run.

stops.name: Milan, the break over neutrality
stops.campa: As Europe goes to war, Mussolini's editorial of 18 October swings without warning from the party's strict neutrality toward active Italian intervention on the Allied side. Avanti! and the Socialist Party he has served denounce him overnight as a traitor to internationalist doctrine and to every column he has written for a decade. On 20 October he resigns as editor, walking out of the paper that made his name, already certain that the coming trenches, not the picket line, are where history is now being decided.
